extracted.intended_audience: general readers, students, comedians, and scholars interested in humor and comedy theory
extracted.subtask_description: Understanding and producing dark (black) humor: a comedic style that makes light of taboo, serious, or painful subject matter to provoke discomfort, serious thought, and amusement. Covers distinctions from related subgenres, tonal strategies, functions, and contextual constraints for acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition — subject matter and aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Dark humor is a style of comedy that makes light of subject matter that is generally considered taboo, particularly subjects that are normally considered serious or painful to discuss, aiming to provoke discomfort, serious thought, and amusement for their audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use taboo or painful topics to produce a mixture of discomfort and amusement; the intent may include provoking thought as well as laughter. Example phrasing from the page: "aiming to provoke discomfort, serious thought, and amusement."

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter scope — what counts as 'dark' topics
rubrics_metrics.description: Covers topics generally considered taboo or serious/painful (e.g., death, suicide, suffering), and can be related to grotesque themes; often relies on topics such as death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When selecting subject matter, prefer subjects that are commonly viewed as serious or taboo; note that some subforms (gallows humor) focus specifically on death or situations reminiscent of dying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from blue comedy/obscenity
rubrics_metrics.description: Dark humor differs from blue comedy—which focuses more on topics such as nudity, sex, and body fluids—and from obscenity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the focus is sexual or explicitly obscene material centered on bodily/sexual topics, classify it as blue/off-color rather than dark humor; dark humor's core is taboo seriousness rather than sexual explicitness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction from gallows humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Whereas the term dark humor is relatively broad, gallows humor tends to be used more specifically in relation to death, or situations that are reminiscent of dying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the label 'gallows humor' when the joke specifically revolves around death or imminent death; use 'dark' or 'black comedy' for a wider set of taboo subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and mechanism — cynicism, skepticism, and satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Breton and critical tradition characterize black humor as laughter arising from cynicism and skepticism, often relying on topics such as death; ties to satire and the grotesque are common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a cynical or skeptical stance or satirical framing to produce the characteristic affect of black humor; grotesque elements may intensify the effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target and ethical orientation — victim vs. victimizer
rubrics_metrics.description: Black humor examples can arise either from a victim with whom the audience empathizes (gallows tradition) or from comedy that mocks the victim and trivializes suffering, which can lead to sympathizing with the victimizer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware whether the humor 'punches up' (targets oppressors/power) or 'punches down' (targets victims); mocking victims risks trivializing suffering and producing ethically problematic effects—whereas empathy-based gallows jokes align with coping and shared endurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satirical modes — grotesque vs. ironic satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Grotesque satire (works by addition) often arouses a harsher, 'green' or despairing laughter (risata verde) and aims to make the horror of a situation felt; ironic satire (works by subtraction) produces a different, often lighter effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose grotesque techniques (exaggeration, accumulation of horror) when the goal is to force confronting the atrocity or despair; use ironic/subtractive satire when a subtler critical distance is desired. Example: grotesque "works by additio[n]" and is linked to the 'risata verde' described by Luttazzi.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social functions — coping, morale, and subversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Black comedy can strengthen the morale of the oppressed, undermine the morale of oppressors, and serve as a coping mechanism for professions that routinely face dark subject matter (police, firefighters, ambulance crews, military, journalists, lawyers, funeral directors).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When using dark humor in work/settings with shared traumatic exposure, recognize its role as coping and group-bonding rather than mere entertainment. Avoid misreading these jokes as harmless when used outside the community context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual and speaker-dependent acceptability
rubrics_metrics.description: The relieving aspect of gallows jokes depends on the context of the joke: whether the joke is being told by the threatened person themselves or by someone else; outsiders may not react the way those with mutual knowledge do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess speaker identity, relationship to the subject, and audience background before delivering dark humor; what is acceptable among insiders (shared experience) can be offensive or misunderstood among outsiders. Paul Lewis's warning and profession-based notes emphasize this constraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience reception correlates and variation
rubrics_metrics.description: Research (2017 Cognitive Processing) suggests that people who appreciate dark humor may have higher IQs, show lower aggression, and resist negative feelings more effectively than those who dislike it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect variability in audience reception; demographic and psychological traits can influence whether dark humor is appreciated. Use caution: empirical correlations do not justify insensitive targeting.
